How much should I charge for a voice-over project?

It depends on length, how you price it, and -- more than most narrators price for -- how the buyer plans to use the recording. The rest of this page works through both pricing shapes on real numbers, not rounded examples.

Script-based work: base fee, then a usage multiplier

Commercial, e-learning, IVR, explainer, and animation scripts are priced per word or per finished minute, then scaled by usage/licensing term. Take a 150-word script at $0.30 a word:

FigureArithmeticResult
Base fee150 words × $0.30$45.00
Finished minutes (at 150 wpm)150 ÷ 1501.00 min

The same $45.00 base fee, every usage term

Usage termMultiplierTotal
Internal / training use only1.0×$45.00
Web / unrestricted digital use1.3×$58.50
Regional broadcast1.8×$81.00
National broadcast2.75×$123.75
Full buyout (all media, in perpetuity)4.0×$180.00

A $135.00 spread on identical recorded audio, from usage term alone -- the recording does not change; what the buyer is licensing does.

Audiobook narration: per finished hour, not per word

A 75,000-word manuscript, narrated at a rate of $250 per finished hour, with no separate editing/proofing/ mastering fee:

FigureArithmeticResult
Estimated finished hours75,000 ÷ 9,3008.06 hours
Narration fee8.06 × $250$2,016.13
Effective rate per word$2,016.13 ÷ 75,000$0.03

9,300 words per finished hour is a commonly cited rule of thumb, not a fixed conversion -- a slower, more heavily produced narration style yields fewer finished hours per manuscript word, and a faster one yields more.

Do this with your own project

The voice-over project rate calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own script or manuscript, your own rate, and your own usage term or editing fee, plus optional rush and exclusivity add-ons for script work. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a voice-over project?

It depends on the script's length, how you price it (per word or per finished minute), and -- critically -- how the buyer plans to use the recording. A 150-word script at $0.30 a word has a base fee of $45.00, but the same script can reasonably run anywhere from $45.00 (internal-only use) to $180.00 (a full buyout) once the usage-term multiplier is applied -- a 4x spread on identical work.

Why does the usage term change the price so much?

A script recorded for one company's internal training video is worth far less to the buyer than the same script running as a national television commercial for a year -- the recording is identical, but what the buyer is licensing is completely different. Rate-guide convention prices usage in tiers for exactly this reason: internal use at the base rate, web use at roughly 1.3x, regional broadcast at roughly 1.8x, national broadcast at roughly 2.75x, and a full buyout at roughly 4x.

How is an audiobook priced differently from a commercial script?

Per finished hour (PFH), the audiobook industry's own convention, most visibly used by ACX -- not per word and not per session hour. A finished hour is estimated from manuscript word count using a commonly cited conversion of roughly 9,300 words per finished hour, then priced against that estimate. A 75,000-word manuscript at $250 per finished hour comes out to roughly 8.06 finished hours and a $2,016.13 narration fee.

No warranty. This page and the calculator it links to are not financial or business advice, and they do not replace a qualified professional. Figures here are starting points from commonly cited rate-guide conventions, not a quote, guarantee, or valuation performed on your behalf. Verify every figure against your own market and negotiate your own project terms. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

vs-a-flat-rate-regardless-of-usage.html.text:
← Voice-Over Project Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. quoting one flat rate regardless of usage

The base fee is the easy part — word count times a rate. The number that actually swings is what the buyer plans to do with the recording, and a flat quote has no line for that at all.

What each approach actually involves

A flat quote prices a script from its word count and a per-word or per-finished-minute rate, then sends that number to the buyer — the same number whether the recording runs once inside a company's internal training portal or nationally on broadcast television for a year.

This calculator prices the base fee the same way, then scales it by the usage/licensing term the buyer actually wants: internal-only use, unrestricted web use, regional broadcast, national broadcast, or a full buyout, using commonly cited voice-over rate-guide multiplier tiers. Because usage is asked for explicitly, the gap between a narrow-use recording and a broadcast or buyout license is priced in instead of given away.

150-word script, $0.30/word ($45.00 base fee — this calculator's shipped default)Flat quote (base fee, every usage)This calculator (usage-scaled)
Internal / training use only$45.00$45.00 — same number
Web / unrestricted digital use$45.00$58.50 — $13.50 more
Regional broadcast$45.00$81.00 — $36.00 more
National broadcast$45.00$123.75 — $78.75 more
Full buyout (all media, in perpetuity)$45.00$180.00 — $135.00 more

Same script, same read, same $45.00 base fee every time. Against a full buyout, the flat quote leaves $135.00 on the table — the buyout rate is four times the flat number, not a rounding difference. A flat habit is not wrong on the internal-only row; it is wrong everywhere past it, and how wrong depends entirely on a question — what usage does the buyer want — the flat quote never asked.

QuestionWhere to answer it
The recording really is internal-only, fixed, one-off — no broadcast or buyout on the table.A flat quote and this calculator's internal-use tier land on the same number. Nothing to lose either way.
The buyer hasn't said yet, or wants web, broadcast, or a buyout license.This calculator — free, instant, private, no account. Ask the usage question before you quote, not after.
You want the underlying rate-guide conventions this calculator applies, not just the output.See the how-to walkthrough for the multiplier tiers worked through on real numbers.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

What does “quoting one flat rate regardless of usage” mean?

Pricing a script from its word count and a per-word or per-finished-minute rate, and sending that number to the buyer no matter what they plan to do with the recording — an internal training video, a public web ad, a regional broadcast spot, a national broadcast campaign, or a full-buyout license that lets them use it anywhere forever. The base fee is the whole quote.

How much does a flat quote actually give away?

On this calculator's own default example — a 150-word script priced per word at $0.30/word, a $45.00 base fee — a flat quote sends $45.00 whichever usage term the buyer wanted. This calculator's usage multiplier instead prices that same base fee at $45.00 for internal-only use, $58.50 for unrestricted web use, $81.00 for regional broadcast, $123.75 for national broadcast, and $180.00 for a full buyout — a $135.00 gap between the flat quote and the real buyout rate, on the identical script and read.

Why does usage change the price at all if the recording itself is identical?

Because what the buyer is licensing is not the recording session, it is the right to use the finished audio a specific way. The same 30-second read is worth far less running once inside one company's internal training portal than running nationally on television for a year. Voice-over rate guides price usage in tiers for exactly this reason — narrower use, lower multiplier; broader or perpetual use, higher multiplier — and a flat quote has no line for that distinction at all.

Is a flat quote ever the right call?

When the usage really is narrow and fixed — a one-off internal-only recording with no broadcast or buyout in play — the flat quote and this calculator's internal-use tier land on the same number, so there is nothing to lose by pricing it either way. The gap only opens once the buyer wants broader or perpetual use, which is exactly when a flat habit keeps quoting the narrow-use number by default.

Are the usage-term multipliers this calculator uses a live rate card?

No. They are commonly cited voice-over rate-guide conventions, exposed as a starting point for your own negotiation, not a fixed or authoritative standard, a quote, or a guarantee of what any buyer will pay. See the calculator's own disclaimer for the exact wording.

vs-voices-com.html.text:
← Voice-over project rate calculator

This calculator vs. Voices.com

Voices.com is a voice-over marketplace: you build a talent profile, upload demos, and audition for jobs clients post there. By publicly available pricing, a free Guest membership gives a limited profile with no ability to actively pursue postings, while a paid membership (reportedly around $499/year for the Premium tier) unlocks full search visibility and audition access. Book a project through the marketplace and Voices.com reportedly takes a 20% commission on top, plus a separate 4-6% payment-processing fee.

That makes Voices.com the right choice for finding clients you don't already have, through a marketplace that handles discovery, auditions, and payment. This page answers a narrower question: for a client you already have -- a returning client, a referral, your own outreach -- what should you actually charge, free, with no membership fee and no commission on what you negotiate directly.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I don't have a client yet -- where do I find one? Voices.com's marketplace, or another casting platform.
I already have a client (or a lead) -- what should I quote them? This calculator -- enter your script or manuscript, get a rate immediately, nothing listed.
What's a typical market rate by project type? Voices.com's own published rate guide, or industry rate-guide resources like the GVAA guide.
What's a defensible rate for my word count, usage term, and rush/exclusivity needs? This calculator's own per-word / per-finished-minute / per-finished-hour math.
Can I get an answer without a profile, a membership fee, or a commission? This calculator -- a static page, no sign-up, no auditions, no cut.
Get a project rate now

This tool needs no account and lists nothing: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your script, manuscript details, and every other figure stay on this device -- nothing is uploaded anywhere, there is no marketplace profile, and no commission on whatever you and your client agree to.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Voices.com?

They solve different problems. Voices.com is a marketplace: you build a profile, upload demos, and audition for jobs that clients post; if you book one, Voices.com handles discovery, escrow, and payment in exchange for a commission. This page is a free calculator: no profile, no auditions, no marketplace fee. You enter your script's word count or an audiobook manuscript's length, pick a pricing method and usage term, and it gives you a project rate to quote a client you already found yourself -- a returning client, a referral, or your own outreach.

What does Voices.com actually charge?

By publicly available pricing, voice talent can join free as a Guest member with a limited profile and no ability to actively pursue postings, or pay for a paid membership (reported around $499/year for the Premium tier) for full search visibility and the ability to submit auditions to client jobs. On top of membership, Voices.com reportedly takes a 20% commission on the value of a booked project, plus a separate 4-6% payment-processing fee depending on payout method -- so on a $1,000 project you would net well under $800 after both. This calculator charges nothing at all and takes no percentage of anything you book.

Does Voices.com price a project the same way this calculator does?

Not the same mechanism. Voices.com clients typically post a job with a budget and voice talent submit competing auditions and quotes, so the price a project settles at is whatever the marketplace's auction dynamic produces -- Voices.com also publishes its own general rate guide as a reference. This calculator has no auction and no marketplace data; it applies commonly cited voice-over rate-guide conventions (a per-word or per-finished-minute base fee scaled by usage/licensing term for script work, or a per-finished-hour rate for audiobooks) to your own numbers, so the starting point is grounded in your own script and rate rather than what another talent happened to bid on a different job.

Is this page affiliated with Voices.com?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Voices.com, and this page is not a review of it. Voices.com is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is for. The membership and commission figures described above are drawn from publicly reported pricing rather than measured by us, and marketplace fees, tiers, and terms change -- check Voices.com's current terms on their site before relying on any number here.
